sermon.title: Vocational Vices and Virtues
sermon.thesis: Ecclesiastes 10–11 walks through ten vocational vices — and their matching virtues. Every one is finally a theology problem: how you work makes visible what you actually believe about God.

outline.body: He who quarries stones is hurt by them, and he who splits logs is endangered by them.
Our work bites back — we labor in cursed ground, among the thorns (Genesis 3:17–19). But the sluggard turns that danger into an excuse: “There is a lion in the streets!” Fortitude works anyway.
If the iron is blunt, and one does not sharpen the edge, he must use more strength, but wisdom helps one to succeed.
Don't just work harder — work wiser. Sharpen the axe; think in systems. (And v. 11: the snake-charmer who acts too late gains nothing — timing matters.)
The words of a wise man's mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him.

The vice is overconfidence — claiming to know more than you know, saying more than you should. “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Proverbs 27:2); “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13).

Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child, and your princes feast in the morning! Happy are you, O land, when your king is the son of the nobility, and your princes feast at the proper time, for strength, and not for drunkenness!

The contrast isn't feasting vs. abstaining — it's feasting in the morning vs. feasting at the proper time, for strength. Appetite running ahead of accomplishment, vs. refueling what you've already earned.
Through sloth the roof sinks in, and through indolence the house leaks.

The most-named vocational problem in all of wisdom literature. But there's a second kind that doesn't look lazy at all — the person always in motion who still isn't doing the thing that matters. The old word is acedia, “the noonday demon”: restlessness, not just torpor. The laziest man in the room may be the busiest.
The realization that I could be simultaneously busy and lazy, that I could be a hectic sluggard, that my busyness was no immunity from laziness, became a life-altering and work-altering insight.
Bread is made for laughter, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.
We do need some way of marking a good day's work — a worker's hunger works for him. Receive the reward with gratitude, not as your due.
Even in your thoughts, do not curse the king, nor in your bedroom curse the rich, for a bird of the air will carry your voice, or some winged creature tell the matter.

Covetousness is an old “thorn” in vocation — you eye another's success, resentment builds, and you talk yourself right out of your own agency. But God's word to Cain still stands: you know what is right; do it.
In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.

“He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap” (v. 4). He isn't wrong that the future is uncertain — he's wrong that uncertainty is a reason to wait. Act boldly; spread your bets (vv. 1–2).

Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.
Light is sweet. Rejoice in your days — and put away vexation — all while remembering you answer to God for every bit of it.
Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, “I have no pleasure in them.”

Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”

Don't presume on tomorrow — and don't keep saying you'll finally get after it tomorrow. Do what you can today. “Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin” (James 4:17).

outline.text: The point: your work is your theology, made visible

outline.body: Every one of these is finally a theology problem. Show me how a person works — how they handle authority, delay, reward, unseen labor, and the gap between sowing and reaping — and I can tell you a good deal about what they actually believe about God. It's no accident that the main biblical word for worship is also the word for work.

The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man. For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.
Why was the wicked servant wicked in the parable of the talents? He had a theology problem — he didn't really know God. Which is why, more than anything, you have to have a clear view of the Lord.

announcements.title: Church Potluck
announcements.body: Theme: Midwest Dinner. What to bring by last name — A–I: a main dish; J–R: a side dish or salad; S–Z: a dessert or drink. Newcomers don't need to bring anything, and bring a cooler if you need to keep something cold.

announcements.title: New to Providence? BBQ
announcements.body: If you've been attending Providence for six months or less, come for an afternoon of food and fellowship at the Gimottys' home (near 119th & Pflumm).

announcements.title: Providence Women's Retreat
announcements.body: Join the women of Providence for a refreshing weekend on The Attributes of God, with special guest speaker Katie Faris — biblical teaching, worship, fellowship, and encouragement. Friday evening (6:30–9pm) through Saturday afternoon (9am–2pm) at the church. $25; registration is open.

announcements.title: Men's Retreat
announcements.body: Men, mark your calendars for our annual Men's Retreat. Meet Justin Lackmacher, founder of Redemption House. Chris and Dov have gotten to know Justin over the years and are absolutely thrilled to have him spend time with the men at Providence. Justin is a former addict, a current minister to addicts, and — as Pastor Chris puts it — has serious Biblical Counseling game.
